topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Nouns, Pronouns, Verbs
concepts: Step 1 — Establish each part of speech with its JOB, using a simple sentence to show all three working together
"Ada kicked the ball." — Ada (noun, names a person), kicked (verb, shows the action), it (a pronoun could replace "the ball": "Ada kicked it").
A part of speech describes the job a word is doing in a sentence. The same word can sometimes do different jobs in different sentences, so use context.
workedExamples: Without pronouns: "Musa took Musa's bag because Musa was going to school." (repetitive, awkward) With pronouns: "Musa took his bag because he was going to school." (smoother)
“Ada carried her bag.” Ada and bag are nouns; carried is a verb; her is a pronoun/determiner referring to Ada.
practiceQuestions: Identify the noun, verb, and pronoun in: "She ate her lunch quickly."
Rewrite this sentence using a pronoun to avoid repetition: "Tunde loves Tunde's dog. Tunde plays with the dog every day."
Identify the nouns and verb in “The pupils opened their books.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Adjectives
concepts: Step 1 — Establish that adjectives describe/give MORE detail about a noun
Adjectives describe or give more information about nouns. Comparatives compare two; superlatives compare three or more.
Many comparatives use -er and superlatives use -est, but longer adjectives often use more/most and irregular forms must be learned in context.
workedExamples: "The dog" (plain) vs "The big, brown dog" (adjectives "big" and "brown" add detail).
tall → taller → tallest; beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful.
practiceQuestions: Add two adjectives to describe "the house."
Identify the adjectives in: "The tall, old man walked slowly." (note: "slowly" describes the verb, not the noun — it's an adverb, not an adjective; a useful early distinction).
Write the comparative and superlative of “bright.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Simple and Compound Sentences
concepts: Step 1 — Establish a simple sentence (one complete idea) vs a compound sentence (two simple sentences joined by "and," "but," or "or")
A complete sentence expresses a complete thought and normally contains a subject and a verb.
A simple sentence has one main independent clause; a compound sentence joins two independent ideas with a suitable coordinator such as and, but, or, so.
workedExamples: Simple: "I like mangoes." Simple: "I like oranges." Compound (joined): "I like mangoes and oranges."
“I finished my work.” is simple. “I finished my work, so I went outside.” is compound.
practiceQuestions: Join these two simple sentences into one compound sentence: "It was raining. We stayed indoors."
Write one simple sentence and one compound sentence about your school.
Write one simple sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension
concepts: Step 1 — Establish literal questions (answer is directly stated) vs inferential questions (answer requires reasoning from clues, not directly stated)
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
A detail answer should be supported by exact information from the passage; an inference combines passage clues with logical reasoning without inventing new facts.
workedExamples: Sample passage: "Chidi woke up early to help his mother prepare for the market. He carried the heavy basket of vegetables to the roadside, where they waited for a bus."
"What did Chidi carry?" → Answer: a heavy basket of vegetables (directly stated).

"Why do you think Chidi woke up early?" → Answer: likely to have enough time to help prepare and get to the market before it got busy or before the goods spoiled — this isn't directly stated, but reasoned from the context.
practiceQuestions: Using the passage above, is "Where did Chidi and his mother wait?" a literal or inferential question? Answer it.
Write one inferential question about the passage, and answer it using reasoning (not a directly stated fact).
State the main idea of a short paragraph in one sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary
concepts: Step 1 — Establish synonyms (same/similar meaning) and antonyms (opposite meaning) with clear paired examples
Vocabulary means understanding and using words accurately in context. A word’s meaning can change with the sentence around it.
Synonyms are close in meaning; antonyms are opposites. Always test the proposed word in the sentence.
workedExamples: Synonym of "happy": glad, joyful. Antonym of "happy": sad.
In “The rapid car passed us,” rapid means fast.
practiceQuestions: Give a synonym for "big."
Give an antonym for "fast."
Choose the correct meaning from context: "The famished dog ate quickly." What does "famished" mean, based on the clue "ate quickly"?

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Writing
concepts: Step 1 — Model a simple descriptive paragraph, annotated

"My classroom is bright and colourful. [general impression] The walls are painted blue, and posters of animals hang everywhere. [sight detail] Every morning, the sound of chattering students fills the room before the teacher arrives. [sound detail]"
Good writing begins with a clear purpose and audience. Plan the main idea before drafting.
workedExamples: Plan three points before writing a paragraph about your school.
Improve “My school is nice. It is nice. I like it.” by adding specific details and removing repetition.
practiceQuestions: Write a short descriptive paragraph (3-4 sentences) about your bedroom, including at least one sight detail and one sound detail.
Write a short narrative paragraph about a fun day you had, using simple/compound sentences correctly.
Write a topic sentence about a memorable day.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Spelling and Dictation
concepts: Step 1 — Establish common tricky spelling patterns for this level
Words often confused: "there/their/they're," "here/hear," "to/too/two."
Spelling is the conventional letter pattern used to write words. Dictation checks careful listening, word boundaries, spelling and punctuation.
workedExamples: necessary can be checked by syllables and visual pattern: nec-es-sar-y.
In dictation, “They’re going home.” requires understanding that they’re means they are.
practiceQuestions: Choose the correct word: "___ going to the market." (There/Their/They're)
Choose the correct word: "I have ___ books." (to/too/two)
Spell “beautiful” and “necessary.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Adverbs, Prepositions, Conjunctions
concepts: Step 1 — Recall adverbs describe HOW/WHEN/WHERE an action happens (often ending in "-ly")
Step 2 — Establish prepositions show position/relationship
Adverbs add information about verbs, adjectives or other adverbs; prepositions show relationships such as place or time; conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses.
workedExamples: "She sings beautifully." (beautifully = adverb, describes HOW she sings)
"The cat is under the table." (under = preposition, shows position)
practiceQuestions: Identify the adverb in: "He ran quickly to school."
Fill in the correct preposition: "The book is ___ the shelf." (on/under/beside — choose based on described position)
Join with a conjunction: "She was tired. She finished her homework." (use "but")

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the rule: singular subjects need singular verbs (often with "-s"), plural subjects need plural verbs (no "-s")
Subject–verb agreement means the verb form must match the subject in number and person.
Find the true subject before choosing the verb; words between subject and verb can distract you.
workedExamples: "The dog barks." (singular dog → barks, with -s) "The dogs bark." (plural dogs → bark, no -s)
“The boy runs.” but “The boys run.”
practiceQuestions: Choose correctly: "The children (plays/play) outside."
Correct this sentence: "My sister go to school every day."
Choose: The list of names (is/are) on the desk.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension
concepts: Step 1 — Extend to SEQUENCING (putting events in the order they happened) and MAIN IDEA identification
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
A detail answer should be supported by exact information from the passage; an inference combines passage clues with logical reasoning without inventing new facts.
workedExamples: Sample passage: "First, Ngozi watered the plants. Then she swept the compound. Finally, she fed the chickens before going to school."
"What did Ngozi do FIRST?" → watered the plants (the word "first" directly signals order).
"What is this passage mainly about?" → Ngozi completing her morning chores before school (not just one detail, but the overall point).
practiceQuestions: Using the passage, what did Ngozi do LAST?
State the main idea of the passage in one sentence.
State the main idea of a short paragraph in one sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary
concepts: Step 1 — Establish homophones (same sound, different meaning/spelling) and compound words (two words joined to make one new word)
Vocabulary means understanding and using words accurately in context. A word’s meaning can change with the sentence around it.
Synonyms are close in meaning; antonyms are opposites. Always test the proposed word in the sentence.
workedExamples: "flower" (a plant) vs "flour" (used for baking) — sound identical, mean different things.
"sun" + "flower" = "sunflower."
practiceQuestions: Give the correct homophone: "I need to ___ (bye/buy) some bread."
Break down "football" into its two smaller words, and explain what the combined word means.
Give a synonym for “rapid.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Writing
concepts: Step 1 — Model an informal letter, annotated

"Dear Grandma, [casual salutation] I hope you are fine. I miss you so much! [warm opening] School has been fun this term — I made a new friend called Amina. [personal news] I can't wait to visit you during the holidays. [closing thought] Love, Tolu [casual closing]"
Good writing begins with a clear purpose and audience. Plan the main idea before drafting.
workedExamples: Plan three points before writing a paragraph about your school.
Improve “My school is nice. It is nice. I like it.” by adding specific details and removing repetition.
practiceQuestions: Write a short informal letter to a friend telling them about your favorite subject in school.
Write a topic sentence about a memorable day.
List three checks to make during revision.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Punctuation
concepts: Step 1 — Establish capitalization rules (start of sentence, proper nouns) and end punctuation (full stop, question mark)
Punctuation shows sentence boundaries, pauses, ownership, quotation and other relationships in writing.
A full stop ends a statement; a comma separates suitable elements but cannot normally join two complete sentences by itself.
workedExamples: Wrong: “It was late, we went home.” Better: “It was late, so we went home.”
“The boy’s book” means the book belongs to one boy; “the boys’ books” refers to more than one boy.
practiceQuestions: Correct this sentence: "my friend ada lives in lagos"
Add the correct end punctuation: "where is your book" (should this end in a full stop or a question mark, and why?)
Correct: She was hungry she ate quickly.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Direct and Indirect Speech (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish direct speech (the EXACT words spoken, in quotation marks) vs indirect speech (reporting what was said, without quotation marks, often changing pronouns/tense)
Direct speech gives the speaker’s exact words; indirect speech reports the message without quoting the exact wording.
When changing to indirect speech, pronouns, time words and verb tense may change to keep the meaning correct from the reporter’s viewpoint.
workedExamples: Direct: Ada said, "I am hungry." Indirect: Ada said that she was hungry. (notice: "I"→"she", "am"→"was")
Direct: She said, “I am tired.” Indirect: She said that she was tired.
practiceQuestions: Convert to indirect speech: Musa said, "I like football."
Convert to direct speech: Tola said that she was tired.
Change to indirect speech: He said, “I will come tomorrow.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Plurals and Comparatives/Superlatives
concepts: Adjectives describe or give more information about nouns. Comparatives compare two; superlatives compare three or more.
Many comparatives use -er and superlatives use -est, but longer adjectives often use more/most and irregular forms must be learned in context.
Plural forms show more than one; regular nouns often add -s/-es, while some are irregular.
workedExamples: child→children (irregular). tall→taller→tallest (regular comparison).
tall → taller → tallest; beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful.
practiceQuestions: Give the plural of "tooth" and "box."
Give the comparative and superlative of "happy."
Write the comparative and superlative of “bright.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce figurative language recognition and TONE (the feeling/mood of a passage)
Sample sentence: "The wind whispered through the trees, and dark clouds gathered ominously overhead."
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
workedExamples: This sentence uses personification ("wind whispered") and creates a tense/eerie TONE through word choice ("ominously," "dark clouds").
If a passage says “Amina carried an umbrella because dark clouds gathered,” we can infer she expected rain, although the passage may not state that exact sentence.
practiceQuestions: Identify the figurative language in: "The stars danced in the night sky."
Is the tone of "The children laughed and played joyfully in the sunshine" happy or sad? Explain using specific words from the sentence.
State the main idea of a short paragraph in one sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce idioms/proverbs (phrases whose meaning isn't literal) and word families
Vocabulary means understanding and using words accurately in context. A word’s meaning can change with the sentence around it.
Synonyms are close in meaning; antonyms are opposites. Always test the proposed word in the sentence.
workedExamples: "It's raining cats and dogs" doesn't mean animals are literally falling — it means it's raining very heavily.
In “The rapid car passed us,” rapid means fast.
practiceQuestions: Explain the meaning of the proverb: "A stitch in time saves nine."
List 3 words in the same word family as "teach" (e.g., teacher, teaching).
Give a synonym for “rapid.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Writing
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce summary writing (very simple level): stating the main point of a short passage in one's own words
Good writing begins with a clear purpose and audience. Plan the main idea before drafting.
Organise ideas in a sensible order, use complete sentences and connect related ideas into paragraphs.
workedExamples: Passage: "Bola practiced her spelling words every evening for a week. On the test day, she scored 100%." Summary: "Bola's regular practice helped her score perfectly on her spelling test."
Plan three points before writing a paragraph about your school.
practiceQuestions: Write a one-sentence summary of: "Musa forgot his umbrella and got soaked walking home in the rain. The next day, he remembered to carry it, and stayed dry."
Write a short essay (narrative OR descriptive, 5-6 sentences) on "My Favorite Day of the Week."
Write a topic sentence about a memorable day.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Verbal Reasoning Foundations
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce odd-one-out and simple analogies as an early foundation for NCEE-style reasoning
Verbal reasoning uses relationships between word meanings, categories, letters or sentence logic.
State the relationship before selecting an answer; this makes distractors easier to reject.
workedExamples: "Apple, Banana, Carrot, Orange" → Carrot is the odd one out, because it's a vegetable while the others are fruits.
"Dog is to Puppy as Cat is to ___?" → Kitten (the pattern: adult animal → baby animal).
practiceQuestions: Find the odd one out: "Chair, Table, Spoon, Bed" and explain why.
Complete the analogy: "Hand is to Glove as Foot is to ___?"
Complete an analogy and state the relationship.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Full Tense Review
concepts: Step 1 — Consolidate present, past, and future, both simple and continuous, with clear side-by-side examples
Simple → Continuous Present → She walks → She is walking Past → She walked → She was walking Future → She will walk → She will be walking
Tense locates an action or state in time and can also show whether it is ongoing or completed.
workedExamples: "By 6pm yesterday, she ___ (finish) her homework." — the word "yesterday" plus "by 6pm" signals a completed past action: "had finished" (though full past perfect is a JSS topic, "finished" as simple past also works at this level for NCEE purposes).
“They have finished” is present perfect: have + finished.
practiceQuestions: Complete: "Right now, she ___ (read) a book." (present continuous)
Complete: "Tomorrow, we ___ (visit) our grandmother." (future)
Identify the tense in “We had left before noon.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Parts of Speech Consolidated
concepts: Step 1 — Recall all parts of speech together in one sentence, labeling each
A part of speech describes the job a word is doing in a sentence. The same word can sometimes do different jobs in different sentences, so use context.
Nouns name people, places, animals, things or ideas; pronouns replace nouns; verbs express actions or states.
workedExamples: "The (article) tall (adjective) boy (noun) quickly (adverb) kicked (verb) the (article) ball (noun) into (preposition) the (article) goal (noun)."
“Ada carried her bag.” Ada and bag are nouns; carried is a verb; her is a pronoun/determiner referring to Ada.
practiceQuestions: Label every word's part of speech in: "She happily sang a beautiful song."
Identify the nouns and verb in “The pupils opened their books.”
Replace repeated nouns with suitable pronouns in a short sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Subject-Verb Agreement (Extended)
concepts: Subject–verb agreement means the verb form must match the subject in number and person.
Find the true subject before choosing the verb; words between subject and verb can distract you.
With present-tense third-person singular subjects, the verb often takes -s, while plural subjects use the base form.
workedExamples: "The basket of apples (is/are) on the table." — the SUBJECT is "basket" (singular), not "apples" — so "is" is correct, even though "apples" (plural) sits right before the verb. This is a genuine trap many students fall into.
“The boy runs.” but “The boys run.”
practiceQuestions: Choose correctly: "The group of students (is/are) going on a trip."
Correct: "The list of items were long."
Choose: The list of names (is/are) on the desk.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce NCEE-style passages combining literal, inferential, and vocabulary-in-context questions together
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
A detail answer should be supported by exact information from the passage; an inference combines passage clues with logical reasoning without inventing new facts.
workedExamples: Sample passage: "Amina had always dreamed of becoming a pilot. Despite her family's initial doubts about a career they considered unconventional for a young girl in her village, she persisted, studying diligently and eventually earning a scholarship to aviation school."
If a passage says “Amina carried an umbrella because dark clouds gathered,” we can infer she expected rain, although the passage may not state that exact sentence.
practiceQuestions: (Literal) What did Amina dream of becoming?
(Inferential) What can you infer about Amina's personality from her actions?
(Vocabulary) What does "unconventional" most likely mean, based on context?

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary
concepts: Step 1 — Extend to one-word substitution (finding a single word that means a whole phrase) and word formation
Vocabulary means understanding and using words accurately in context. A word’s meaning can change with the sentence around it.
Synonyms are close in meaning; antonyms are opposites. Always test the proposed word in the sentence.
workedExamples: "A person who studies stars" = astronomer. "A place where books are kept" = library.
In “The rapid car passed us,” rapid means fast.
practiceQuestions: Give a one-word substitute for "a person who cannot read or write."
Form a noun from "educate" using a suffix.
Give a synonym for “rapid.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Writing
concepts: Step 1 — Model a full narrative composition at NCEE level
[Full narrative essay following opening-rising action-climax-resolution-conclusion, similar structure to JSS1's model but with vocabulary appropriate to Primary 6 level.]
Good writing begins with a clear purpose and audience. Plan the main idea before drafting.
workedExamples: Plan three points before writing a paragraph about your school.
Improve “My school is nice. It is nice. I like it.” by adding specific details and removing repetition.
practiceQuestions: Write a full narrative essay (150 words) titled "A Day I Will Always Remember."
Write a topic sentence about a memorable day.
List three checks to make during revision.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Grammar Accuracy: Articles
concepts: Articles come before nouns. “a” and “an” introduce one non-specific countable noun; “the” points to a specific or already-known noun.
Choose a or an by sound, not simply by the first written letter: an hour, a university.
Some plural or uncountable nouns take no article when speaking generally.
workedExamples: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) vs "a university" (consonant sound despite vowel letter).
“She is an honest girl” because honest begins with a vowel sound.
practiceQuestions: Choose "a" or "an": ___ orange, ___ hour, ___ uniform.
Choose: a/an hour.
Choose: a/an university.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Direct/Indirect Speech (Full)
concepts: Direct speech gives the speaker’s exact words; indirect speech reports the message without quoting the exact wording.
When changing to indirect speech, pronouns, time words and verb tense may change to keep the meaning correct from the reporter’s viewpoint.
Questions in indirect speech use statement word order and normally lose quotation marks and the direct question mark.
workedExamples: Direct: She asked, "Where are you going?" Indirect: She asked where I was going. (notice: question word order changes, and no question mark in indirect speech)
Direct: She said, “I am tired.” Indirect: She said that she was tired.
practiceQuestions: Convert to indirect speech: He said, "I will come tomorrow."
Convert to indirect speech: She asked, "What is your name?"
Change to indirect speech: He said, “I will come tomorrow.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Active and Passive Voice (Introductory)
concepts: In active voice, the subject performs the action; in passive voice, the receiver of the action becomes the grammatical subject.
To form a basic passive sentence, use an appropriate form of be + past participle, preserving the original tense.
Use passive voice when the action or receiver is more important than the doer, but do not change the underlying meaning.
workedExamples: Active: "The boy kicked the ball." Passive: "The ball was kicked by the boy."
Active: “The boy kicked the ball.” Passive: “The ball was kicked by the boy.”
practiceQuestions: Convert to passive: "The teacher taught the lesson."
Change to passive: The chef cooked the meal.
Identify whether a sentence is active or passive.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Conjunctions and Linking Words
concepts: Adverbs add information about verbs, adjectives or other adverbs; prepositions show relationships such as place or time; conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses.
Ask what job the word performs in the sentence instead of judging only by its spelling.
Conjunctions show relationships such as addition, contrast, cause or choice, so choose one that matches the meaning.
workedExamples: "Although it was raining, we went out." vs "We went out because it stopped raining." (Note the different relationship each conjunction signals: contrast vs cause.)
“She ran quickly across the field because she was late.” quickly is an adverb, across is a preposition, because is a conjunction.
practiceQuestions: Join with "because": "She was happy. She passed her exam."
Join with "although": "He was tired. He finished the race."
Identify the adverb and preposition in “The dog slept quietly under the table.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce figures of speech and author's purpose/tone at this level
Sample sentence: "The classroom was as quiet as a graveyard during the test."
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
workedExamples: If a passage says “Amina carried an umbrella because dark clouds gathered,” we can infer she expected rain, although the passage may not state that exact sentence.
If the question asks for two barriers and the passage names cost and poor network, both must appear in the answer.
practiceQuestions: Identify the figure of speech in the sentence above (simile — comparison using "as").
What tone does this sentence create — tense/serious, or relaxed/happy? Explain using the specific comparison used.
State the main idea of a short paragraph in one sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce idioms and proverbs, plus confusable words
Vocabulary means understanding and using words accurately in context. A word’s meaning can change with the sentence around it.
Synonyms are close in meaning; antonyms are opposites. Always test the proposed word in the sentence.
workedExamples: "affect" (verb, to influence) vs "effect" (noun, a result) — "The rain will affect the match" vs "The effect of the rain was a delay."
In “The rapid car passed us,” rapid means fast.
practiceQuestions: Explain the meaning of "Actions speak louder than words."
Choose correctly: "The medicine had a positive (affect/effect) on her health."
Give a synonym for “rapid.”

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Formal Letter
concepts: A formal letter is written for an official purpose and uses respectful, clear language.
Its structure normally includes sender’s address, date, recipient’s title/address where required, salutation, heading/subject, organised body, closing and name/signature.
Each paragraph should have one purpose: introduce the reason, give needed details, and close with the requested action or thanks.
workedExamples: "[Sender's address] [Date] The Headmistress, [school name]. Dear Madam, REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO ORGANIZE A READING CLUB. I am writing to request permission to start a reading club... Yours faithfully, [Name]"
A request to a headteacher should clearly state what is requested and why, without slang.
practiceQuestions: Write a formal letter to your headteacher requesting a new football for the school team.
List the main parts of a formal letter.
Write a suitable heading for a letter requesting library books.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Expository Composition
concepts: Expository writing explains a topic or process clearly rather than telling a fictional story.
Organise the explanation in a logical order, using topic sentences and linking words such as first, next, because and finally.
Use precise details and examples; remove unrelated opinions that do not help explain the topic.
workedExamples: "How to Plant a Seed" — a step-by-step explanation, no opinion.
To explain how to plant a seed, present materials and steps in order from preparing soil to watering.
practiceQuestions: Write an expository paragraph explaining how to make a simple meal you know well.
Write an outline for “How to prepare for school.”
Give three linking words useful in expository writing.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Verbal Reasoning Integration
concepts: Verbal reasoning asks you to notice a relationship between words, not merely remember a definition. Before choosing an option, name the relationship you are using.
For sentence completion, read the whole sentence first. Decide what meaning is missing, then test each option in the sentence. Grammar and meaning must both fit.
For opposites, an antonym must reverse the important meaning of the target word. A word that is merely different is not automatically an opposite.
For analogies, read the first pair as a sentence that states the relationship, such as “a teacher teaches a student.” Apply that same relationship to the second pair.
A reliable verbal-reasoning answer survives a check: you can state the relationship in words and explain why the distractors do not fit it.
workedExamples: Sentence completion: “The opposite of generous is ___: kind, selfish, happy.” Generous means willing to give. Selfish describes being mainly concerned with oneself, so it reverses the important idea. “Kind” is close to generous, while “happy” is unrelated. Answer: selfish.
Analogy: “Teacher is to Student as Doctor is to ___.” State the relationship first: a teacher teaches a student. A doctor treats a patient. Therefore the missing word is patient.
Analogy check: “Bird is to Nest as Bee is to ___.” The relationship is animal to its home. A bee lives in a hive, so hive completes the same relationship.
practiceQuestions: Complete and explain: The opposite of “ancient” is ___ (modern / old / historic).
State the relationship first, then complete: Author is to Book as Composer is to ___.
Complete the sentence using meaning and grammar: “Because the road was flooded, the driver moved very ___.” (carefully / yesterday / blue)
Explain why “selfish” is a better opposite of “generous” than “happy”.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Grammar — Full Punctuation and Error Correction
topics.strand: Grammar — Full Punctuation and Error Correction
concepts: Punctuation shows sentence boundaries, pauses, ownership, quotation and other relationships in writing.
A full stop ends a statement; a comma separates suitable elements but cannot normally join two complete sentences by itself.
Apostrophes can show possession or omitted letters, but they are not used simply to make ordinary plurals.
workedExamples: Wrong: "It was late, we went home." Correct: "It was late, so we went home."
Wrong: “It was late, we went home.” Better: “It was late, so we went home.”
practiceQuestions: Correct: "She was hungry she ate quickly."
Correct: "The boys books are on the table." (apostrophe — possession)
Correct: She was hungry she ate quickly.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Sentence Transformation
topics.strand: Grammar — Full Punctuation and Error Correction
concepts: Sentence transformation changes the form of a sentence while preserving the intended meaning.
The required connector or structure controls how clauses are rearranged; check pronouns, tense and punctuation after transforming.
A correct transformed sentence must be grammatical and keep the same logical relationship such as cause, contrast or result.
workedExamples: Combine using a conjunction: "He is poor. He is happy." → "Although he is poor, he is happy."
He is poor. He is happy. → Although he is poor, he is happy.
practiceQuestions: Combine: "She studied hard. She passed the exam." (using "so")
Combine two sentences using although.
Rewrite two cause-and-effect sentences using because.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Reading Comprehension — Full NCEE-Style Practice
concepts: Sample passage (timed practice style): "The introduction of mobile phones has transformed communication in rural Nigerian communities, allowing farmers to check market prices remotely and families to stay connected across long distances. However, concerns about network reliability and the cost of maintaining phones remain significant barriers for many households."
Read a comprehension passage for meaning before answering. First identify the main idea, then locate details and clues for inference.
A detail answer should be supported by exact information from the passage; an inference combines passage clues with logical reasoning without inventing new facts.
workedExamples: If a passage says “Amina carried an umbrella because dark clouds gathered,” we can infer she expected rain, although the passage may not state that exact sentence.
If the question asks for two barriers and the passage names cost and poor network, both must appear in the answer.
practiceQuestions: What has mobile phone use allowed farmers to do?
What are the TWO barriers mentioned?
What does "barriers" mean in this context?
What is the overall topic of this passage?

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Vocabulary — Comprehensive Review
concepts: Vocabulary questions test meaning in context. The safest method is to identify the meaning needed in the sentence or expression before looking at the options.
A synonym has the same or nearly the same meaning in the given context. Two words can be related without being synonyms, so test them in a sentence.
An antonym expresses the opposite meaning. Check the exact sense being used: the opposite of “generous” is “selfish” or “stingy,” not simply any negative word.
A one-word substitution replaces a longer description with one precise word. The replacement must preserve the whole meaning, not only part of it.
An idiom has a meaning that cannot always be obtained by reading each word literally. Use the situation around the idiom to infer the intended meaning.
During review, compare close words and explain why one fits. This prevents guessing from familiarity.
workedExamples: Synonym: “The examination was difficult.” In this sentence, “hard” can replace “difficult” without changing the main meaning. Therefore “hard” is a suitable synonym.
Antonym: “Ada is generous with her food.” The opposite idea is being unwilling to share. “Selfish” or “stingy” fits; “happy” does not reverse the meaning.
One-word substitution: “a person who loves books” can be called a bibliophile. For Primary 6, AVORA first teaches the meaning before expecting the label.
Idiom: “break the ice” does not mean breaking frozen water. In a social situation it means doing or saying something that makes people feel more comfortable and starts interaction.
practiceQuestions: Give a synonym for “difficult” and use it in a sentence.
Give an antonym for “generous” and explain the contrast.
What does “break the ice” mean in this sentence: “The teacher told a funny story to break the ice on the first day”?
Choose the closest meaning of “rapid”: slow / quick / weak / quiet, and explain your choice.
topics.completionBasis: AVORA-authored completion from the supplied Primary 6 English review source; expands the source questions into explicit synonym, antonym, substitution and idiom teaching.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Writing — Summary and Full Composition Practice
topics.strand: Writing — Summary and Full Composition Practice
concepts: A summary keeps the central meaning while removing repetition, examples and unnecessary detail.
Read the full passage first, identify the main point and essential supporting ideas, then restate them briefly in your own words.
A summary should not introduce a new opinion or information that was not in the passage.
workedExamples: Passage: "Chidi trained every day for the school race, even when tired. On race day, his effort paid off as he won first place." Summary: "Chidi's consistent training led to his race victory."
“Chidi trained daily despite tiredness and won the race.” can be summarised as “Chidi’s consistent training led to his victory.”
practiceQuestions: Summarize in one sentence: "Ngozi saved a little money each week from her allowance. After a year, she had enough to buy her mother a special gift."
Write a full composition (any type — narrative, descriptive, or expository, 150-200 words) on a topic of your choice.
Summarise a three-sentence paragraph in one sentence.

topics.subject: English Studies
topics.title: Full NCEE-Style Objective Practice (Combined)
concepts: Practice Questions (mixed, timed-practice style):
practiceQuestions: Choose the correct word: "She is (a/an) honest girl."
Identify the tense: "They have finished their homework."
Choose the antonym of "ancient": (modern/old/ancient-looking)
Complete the analogy: "Kitten is to Cat as Puppy is to ___?"
Correct the sentence: "Him and me went to the shop."

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Living and Non-Living Things
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the TEST for classifying something as living: does it grow, breathe, feed, move, and reproduce?
Living things carry out life processes such as feeding, respiration, growth, response, reproduction and removal of wastes; non-living things do not carry out these processes by themselves.
Movement alone does not prove that something is living: a car moves because an external system powers it.
workedExamples: Is a rock living or non-living? Test: does it grow? No. Does it breathe/feed/reproduce? No. → Non-living. Is a tree living or non-living? Test: does it grow? Yes. Does it need food (nutrients/water) and produce seeds? Yes. → Living.
A fish grows, feeds, respires and reproduces, so it is living.
practiceQuestions: Classify as living or non-living, explaining using the test: a car, a fish, a chair, a plant.
Classify a mushroom and explain two life characteristics.
Why is movement alone not enough to classify something as living?

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Human Body — Major Organs (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish a few key organs and their SPECIFIC function, not just names
The heart pumps blood around the body. The lungs help us breathe (take in oxygen, release carbon dioxide). The brain controls thinking and all body actions. The stomach helps digest food.
An organ is a body part made of tissues that performs a particular job. A body system is a group of organs working together.
workedExamples: During exercise, breathing and heartbeat increase because muscles need more oxygen and nutrients.
Food is broken down by the digestive system and absorbed nutrients are transported by the blood.
practiceQuestions: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
Which organ helps you breathe?
State the function of the heart and lungs.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Plants — Parts and Functions
concepts: Roots anchor plants and absorb water/minerals; stems support and transport materials; leaves make food using light; flowers aid reproduction.
A structure’s function explains why damage to that part affects the whole plant.
Plants need suitable water, air, light and nutrients for healthy growth.
workedExamples: Roots absorb water and nutrients from soil; the stem supports the plant and transports water; leaves make food using sunlight (photosynthesis, simply put as "leaves make food using sunlight"); flowers help the plant reproduce.
If roots are badly damaged, water uptake falls and the plant may wilt.
practiceQuestions: Which part of a plant absorbs water from the soil?
Which part of a plant makes food?
State two functions of roots.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: States of Matter
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the three states by their SHAPE/VOLUME behavior

Solid: has a fixed shape and volume (e.g., a stone). Liquid: has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container (e.g., water). Gas: has no fixed shape or volume, spreads to fill any space (e.g., air).
Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take the container’s shape; gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.
workedExamples: Ice melts from solid to liquid when heated.
Water vapour cools and condenses into liquid water.
practiceQuestions: Classify as solid, liquid, or gas: ice, air, milk, wood.
What happens to ice when it melts — which state does it change to?
Classify air, milk and wood by state.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Nigeria's States and Geopolitical Zones
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the SIX geopolitical zones as a way of grouping Nigeria's 36 states
Nigeria has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja), grouped into six geopolitical zones: North West, North East, North Central, South West, South East, South South.
Nigeria has 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Geopolitical zones are six broad regional groupings used to organise states for discussion and administration.
workedExamples: Lagos State belongs to the South West geopolitical zone.
Abuja is in the Federal Capital Territory and is associated geographically with the North Central region.
practiceQuestions: Name the six geopolitical zones of Nigeria.
Which zone is Lagos State part of?
Name the six geopolitical zones.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Family and Community Roles
concepts: A family is a group of people connected by birth, marriage, adoption or care who support one another. A community is a group of people who live, learn or work in the same area or share common institutions.
A role is the part a person plays in a group. A responsibility is a duty that the person is expected to carry out. Roles can differ, but every member should contribute responsibly.
Children have age-appropriate responsibilities such as respecting others, keeping personal and shared spaces tidy, caring for school materials and completing assigned chores safely.
Adults and community leaders also have responsibilities, such as caring for children, providing guidance, maintaining order, supporting community development and protecting public property.
Communities work well through cooperation, respect for rules, peaceful problem-solving, sanitation, honesty and participation in useful communal activities.
A responsible action should be judged by its effect on other people and on shared property. Good citizenship begins with everyday choices at home, school and in the community.
workedExamples: A class is preparing for clean-up day. One learner sweeps only his desk while rubbish remains around the shared classroom. His personal area is clean, but his community role also includes helping protect the shared environment. A responsible action is to join the agreed class clean-up.

A younger child cannot safely carry a heavy water container. Responsibility does not mean doing unsafe work. The child can take an age-appropriate role, such as arranging light items or informing an adult that help is needed.
Neighbours organise a monthly sanitation exercise. Joining the exercise, disposing of waste properly and protecting the drainage are examples of cooperation for community wellbeing.
practiceQuestions: Name two age-appropriate responsibilities a child can carry out at home and explain why each matters.
Give two ways members of a community can work together to improve their environment.
A child sees someone damaging a public tap. What responsible action should the child take?
Explain the difference between a role and a responsibility using a school example.
topics.completionBasis: AVORA-authored completion from the supplied Primary 5 General Paper source and NERDC National Values themes on family, community, rules and responsibilities.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Citizenship — Rights and Responsibilities (Introductory)
concepts: Identify the value, right, duty or community principle involved before choosing an action.
Consider how the action affects other people, public property and peaceful community life.
Choose a responsible action and explain its likely consequence.
workedExamples: A right is something you are entitled to (e.g., the right to education). A responsibility is something you are expected to do (e.g., respecting others' property).
Use a home or school situation to identify a responsibility.
practiceQuestions: Name one right every child has.
Name one responsibility a student has at school.
Name the principle involved.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Human Body Systems (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish each system by its FUNCTION, not just its name

The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients the body can use (mouth→stomach→intestines). The respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide (nose/lungs). The circulatory system moves blood (carrying oxygen and nutrients) around the body via the heart and blood vessels.
An organ is a body part made of tissues that performs a particular job. A body system is a group of organs working together.
workedExamples: During exercise, breathing and heartbeat increase because muscles need more oxygen and nutrients.
Food is broken down by the digestive system and absorbed nutrients are transported by the blood.
practiceQuestions: Which system breaks down food?
Which organ is central to the circulatory system?
State the function of the heart and lungs.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Plants and Animals — Classification Basics
concepts: Classification groups organisms using shared observable features. A useful rule must fit every member of the group.
Animals can be grouped by features such as body covering, habitat or backbone; plants can be grouped by observable structures and growth forms.
Use more than one characteristic when a single feature could place very different organisms together.
workedExamples: Animals can be classified as vertebrates (have a backbone, e.g., fish, birds, mammals) or invertebrates (no backbone, e.g., insects, worms).
Birds have feathers, while mammals have hair/fur and feed their young with milk.
practiceQuestions: Classify as vertebrate or invertebrate: a snake, a butterfly, a dog, a spider.
Give one feature used to classify animals.
Place fish and goat into different groups and state your rule.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Simple Machines and Everyday Technology
concepts: A simple machine makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force; common examples include lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, screw and wedge.
Machines do not remove work completely; they trade force for distance or change how the force is applied.
Use tools safely for their intended purpose and identify the simple-machine principle involved.
workedExamples: A lever (like a see-saw) makes lifting easier by using a pivot point. A pulley (like on a well) makes lifting heavy objects easier by changing the direction of force needed.
A ramp is an inclined plane that lets a load be raised with less force over a longer distance.
practiceQuestions: Name a simple machine used to lift heavy water from a well.
Give an example of a lever used in everyday life.
Name the simple machine in a ramp.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Energy and Forces (Introductory)
concepts: A force is a push or pull that can change motion, direction or shape.
Energy is the ability to cause change or do work and appears in forms such as light, heat, sound, electrical and movement energy.
Energy can be transferred or changed from one form to another, while friction and other forces affect motion.
workedExamples: Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward the Earth — this is why a dropped ball falls down, not up or sideways.
A battery-powered torch changes chemical energy in the battery to electrical energy and then light/heat.
practiceQuestions: What force causes a dropped object to fall to the ground?
Name one source of renewable energy (e.g., sunlight, wind).
Give two effects a force can have.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Health and Hygiene
concepts: Health is a state of physical and mental wellbeing. Hygiene means habits that help keep the body and surroundings clean and reduce the spread of disease.

Germs are tiny disease-causing organisms or agents that can spread through dirty hands, contaminated food or water, droplets from coughing and sneezing, and unclean surroundings. We cannot usually see them, so prevention depends on good habits.
Handwashing works best when hands are washed with clean running water and soap, including palms, backs of hands, between fingers and around nails, then rinsed and dried cleanly.
Respiratory hygiene means covering a cough or sneeze with a tissue or the inside of the elbow, disposing of the tissue safely and cleaning the hands afterwards.

A balanced diet contains appropriate amounts from different food groups so the body receives energy, body-building nutrients, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Eating only one type of food repeatedly is not balanced.
Safe food and water practices include using clean water, washing foods that should be washed, keeping utensils clean, cooking food properly where necessary and protecting food from flies and dirt.
Regular exercise, enough rest, personal cleanliness and a clean environment work together with good nutrition to support health.
workedExamples: Before eating, Chika has visible dirt on her hands after playing outside. Rinsing quickly without soap may leave germs behind. A safer routine is to wash thoroughly with soap and clean running water before touching food.
A meal contains rice only. Rice provides useful energy, but a balanced meal needs other nutrients too. Adding beans or another protein source and vegetables or fruit gives a wider range of nutrients.

Tunde coughs directly into his palm and then holds a shared classroom ruler. Germs can move from his hand to the ruler. Coughing into the elbow or a tissue and cleaning the hands reduces this route of spread.
practiceQuestions: Name two ways to reduce the spread of germs and explain how each works.
Why is a balanced diet better than eating only one favourite food every day?
What should you do after coughing into a tissue?
Give one food-safety habit and one environmental-hygiene habit.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Nigeria's Government Structure (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the three tiers of government by their SCOPE (what area each governs)
Federal government (governs the whole country), State government (governs one state), Local government (governs a smaller local area within a state).
Nigeria operates three tiers of government: federal, state and local government.
workedExamples: National defence is a federal responsibility because it concerns the whole country.
Local sanitation and community markets may involve local government responsibilities.
practiceQuestions: Name the three tiers of government in Nigeria.
Which tier of government would handle a matter affecting the ENTIRE country (e.g., national defense)?
Name the three tiers.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: National Symbols and Their Meaning
concepts: National symbols represent shared identity and values and should be treated with respect.
The Nigerian flag is green-white-green; the green is commonly taught as representing natural wealth/agriculture and the white as peace.
Symbols such as the coat of arms, anthem and pledge communicate national identity, unity and civic ideals.
workedExamples: The Nigerian flag has green-white-green stripes: green represents the nation's rich agriculture/natural wealth, white represents peace and unity.
Recognising the flag is not enough; explain what its colours are intended to represent.
practiceQuestions: What do the colors of the Nigerian flag represent?
Name Nigeria's national anthem's first line (or describe its general theme of unity/pride).
Describe the Nigerian flag.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizens
concepts: A right is a freedom or protection a person is entitled to under the law and society. A responsibility is a duty a person should carry out toward other people, the community and the country.
Rights and responsibilities belong together. Having a right does not mean a person may harm other people or prevent them from enjoying their own rights.
Examples of civic rights discussed at this level include access to education, freedom of expression within the law, fair treatment and protection of life and dignity.

Examples of responsibilities include obeying lawful rules, respecting the rights of others, protecting public property, keeping the environment clean, helping maintain peace and participating responsibly in community life.
Public property belongs to everyone collectively. Damaging a public school desk, road sign, water facility or health-centre property harms the whole community and is irresponsible.
Responsible citizenship also requires peaceful disagreement. A person can express an opinion without insulting, threatening or attacking others.
When a right appears to conflict with another person’s safety or rights, AVORA asks: What is the right? What is the duty? Who could be affected? What action respects both as far as possible?
workedExamples: A learner has a right to learn in school. The learner also has a responsibility not to disrupt the lesson so that classmates can enjoy the same right to learn.

Citizens may express opinions, but spreading a dangerous false alarm that causes panic can harm others. Responsible expression means using the freedom without violating other people’s safety and rights.
A public tap is damaged deliberately. Because it serves many people, protecting and reporting damage to it is a responsibility toward the community.
practiceQuestions: Name one right and one responsibility of a citizen, then explain how they can support each other.
Why is protecting public property a civic responsibility?
A learner disagrees with a class rule. Give a peaceful and responsible way to raise the concern.
Explain why having a right does not mean ignoring the rights of other people.
topics.completionBasis: AVORA-authored completion from the supplied Primary 6 General Paper source and NERDC National Values/Civic Education themes on rights, duties and responsible citizenship.

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Nigeria's History — Key Milestones
concepts: Historical milestones are important events used to organise a country’s story through time.
Nigeria gained independence from British colonial rule on 1 October 1960.
A date should be connected to what happened and why it mattered, rather than memorised as an isolated number.
workedExamples: Nigeria gained independence from British colonial rule on October 1, 1960.
1 October 1960 marks Nigeria’s independence.
practiceQuestions: In what year did Nigeria gain independence?
Name one significant event in Nigeria's history you have learned about.
What happened on 1 October 1960?

topics.subject: General Paper
topics.title: Current Affairs and General Knowledge (NCEE-Relevant)
concepts: General knowledge includes important facts about Nigeria and the world that are relatively stable, while current affairs concerns important events and office-holders that can change with time.
For a fact that can change, always attach a date and verify it from a reliable current source. A current office-holder should never be treated as a fact that can never change.

As of 14 September 2026, the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria is Bola Ahmed Tinubu. This is a dated current-affairs fact and must be re-verified in a later release before it is taught as current.
Nigeria is in West Africa. Its land neighbours are Benin to the west, Niger to the north, Chad to the north-east and Cameroon to the east. Nigeria also has a southern coastline on the Gulf of Guinea.
Abuja is Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory and seat of the federal government. Stable national facts should be distinguished from changing facts such as the names of current office-holders.
In an exam, read the wording carefully: a question asking for a current office-holder requires up-to-date knowledge, while a question about a capital, neighbour or historical date may be stable.
workedExamples: Question: “Name one country that shares a land border with Nigeria.” Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon are all valid examples. Ghana is in West Africa but does not share a land border with Nigeria.

Question: “Who is the current President of Nigeria?” AVORA checks the date first. For this release, verified 14 September 2026, the answer is Bola Ahmed Tinubu. The date matters because the office-holder can change.

Question: “What is the capital of Nigeria?” Abuja is a stable general-knowledge answer. This is different from a current-affairs office-holder question because the capital is not expected to change frequently.
practiceQuestions: Name two countries that share a land border with Nigeria.
Explain the difference between a current-affairs fact and a stable general-knowledge fact.
What is Nigeria’s capital?
Why should the name of a current office-holder be checked with a date before an exam?
