topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Whole Numbers
concepts: Step 1 — Build place value from what's already familiar (tens, hundreds) outward

Every digit's value depends on WHERE it sits. In 45,326: the "4" sits in the ten-thousands spot, so it's worth 40,000 — not just "4." Let's build this step by step using a place value chart: Ten-Thousands → Thousands → Hundreds → Tens → Units 4 → 5 → 3 → 2 → 6
Step 1 — Establish the method: compare digit by digit, starting from the LEFT (the biggest place value)
workedExamples: Write 45,326 in expanded form (showing what each digit is really worth): 40,000 + 5,000 + 300 + 20 + 6 = 45,326

72,408 — read as "seventy-two thousand, four hundred and eight." Notice: there's a ZERO in the tens place, so we don't say "seventy-two thousand, four hundred and zero eight" — the zero is silent, just a placeholder.

Compare 34,521 and 34,498. Start from the left: both have "3" in ten-thousands, both have "4" in thousands — tie so far. Next: 5 vs 4 in hundreds — 5 is bigger, so 34,521 > 34,498. We didn't even need to look further right once we found a difference.
practiceQuestions: Write 63,915 in expanded form.
What is the value of the digit 7 in 27,481?
Write in words: 90,204 (careful with the zero — how should it be read?).
Which is bigger: 56,204 or 56,240? Explain using the digit-by-digit method.
Order from smallest to largest: 12,890; 12,098; 12,908.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Addition and Subtraction of Large Whole Numbers
concepts: Step 1 — Recall WHY we regroup: when a column adds to 10 or more, we can't write two digits in one column, so we carry the extra ten to the next column
Step 1 — Recall WHY we borrow: when the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit in a column, we bring one "ten" over from the next column left
Addition combines quantities; subtraction finds what remains or the difference between quantities.
workedExamples: 4,586 + 2,749 Units: 6+9=15 → write 5, carry 1 (that 1 means "one ten") Tens: 8+4+1(carried)=13 → write 3, carry 1 Hundreds: 5+7+1=13 → write 3, carry 1 Thousands: 4+2+1=7 Result: 7,335

6,203 − 2,847 Units: 3−7, can't do it — borrow from tens: tens digit (0) is also empty, so borrow travels further left to hundreds (2 becomes 1), tens becomes 10, then units borrows from tens (10 becomes 9): 13−7=6 Tens: 9−4=5 Hundreds: 1−8, can't do it — borrow from thousands: thousands (6 becomes 5), hundreds becomes 11: 11−8=3 Thousands: 5−2=3 Result: 3,356
practiceQuestions: Add: 3,847 + 2,956, showing every carry.
Subtract: 5,402 − 1,867, showing every borrowing step.
Subtract: 8,000 − 3,456 (careful — multiple zeros require borrowing to travel far left).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Multiplication of Whole Numbers
concepts: Step 1 — Establish that multiplying by a 2-digit number means multiplying by the TENS part and the UNITS part separately, then adding the results
Multiplication is repeated equal grouping and can be broken apart using place value.
The distributive idea lets us multiply a number by parts, then add the partial products.
workedExamples: 234 × 23 Break 23 into 20 + 3. 234 × 3 = 702 234 × 20 = 4,680 (this is 234×2, then a zero added since we're really multiplying by 20) Add: 702 + 4,680 = 5,382
practiceQuestions: Multiply: 312 × 14, showing the breakdown into tens and units.
Multiply: 456 × 32.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Division of Whole Numbers
concepts: Step 1 — Establish what a remainder means: what's LEFT OVER when a number doesn't divide exactly
Division asks how many equal groups can be made or how large each equal share is.
Long division works by dividing one place-value part at a time, multiplying back, subtracting, and bringing down the next digit.
workedExamples: 47 ÷ 5. How many times does 5 fit into 47? 5×9=45 (fits 9 times), with 47−45=2 left over. 47 ÷ 5 = 9 remainder 2.
If 47 sweets are shared equally among 5 children, each gets 9 sweets, and 2 sweets are left over (not enough to give each child one more).
practiceQuestions: Divide: 58 ÷ 6, stating the remainder.
83 oranges are shared among 7 baskets equally. How many oranges per basket, and how many are left over?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Factors and Multiples (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish "factor" using the sharing idea, and "multiple" using repeated counting
A factor of a number divides into it exactly (no remainder). Multiples of a number are what you get counting up in that number's steps (like counting in 5s: 5,10,15,20...).
A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is produced by multiplying the number by a whole number.
workedExamples: Factors of 12: test each number 1-12 for exact division: 1✓,2✓,3✓,4✓,6✓,12✓ (5,7,8,9,10,11 don't divide exactly). Factors: 1,2,3,4,6,12.
Factors of 18 include 1,2,3,6,9,18; multiples of 18 begin 18,36,54.
practiceQuestions: List the factors of 18.
List the first 5 multiples of 7.
Find the LCM of 4 and 6 (recall: list multiples of each, find the first one they share).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Fractions
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the THREE forms using a visual: a proper fraction is less than one whole; an improper fraction is one whole or more, written as a top-heavy fraction; a mixed number is the same amount as an improper fraction, written as a whole number plus a proper fraction
A fraction represents equal parts of a whole or of a quantity. The denominator tells how many equal parts make the whole; the numerator tells how many parts are considered.
Equivalent fractions name the same quantity with different-sized equal parts. Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number to create an equivalent fraction.
workedExamples: 7/3 means 7 divided into groups of 3. 7÷3=2 remainder 1, so 7/3 = 2 whole groups plus 1/3 left over = 2⅓.
3¼: multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator: (3×4)+1=13, keep the same denominator: 13/4.
Is 2/3 the same as 6/9? Multiply top and bottom of 2/3 by 3: 2×3=6, 3×3=9 → yes, 2/3=6/9.
practiceQuestions: Convert 9/4 to a mixed number.
Convert 5⅔ to an improper fraction.
Is 8/8 proper, improper, or does it equal exactly one whole? Explain.
Find an equivalent fraction to 3/5 with a denominator of 20.
Are 4/6 and 2/3 equivalent? Show your check.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Addition and Subtraction of Fractions
concepts: Step 1 — Recall why fractions need the same denominator before adding, using a visual: you can't add "3 fifths" and "2 thirds" directly because the "pieces" are different sizes
Addition combines quantities; subtraction finds what remains or the difference between quantities.
Align digits by place value before using the written method, so ones are combined with ones, tens with tens, and so on.
workedExamples: ⅓ + ¼: find a common denominator (12): ⅓=4/12, ¼=3/12. Add: 4/12+3/12=7/12.
2½ − 1¼: convert to improper fractions first: 2½=5/2, 1¼=5/4. Common denominator=4: 5/2=10/4. Subtract: 10/4−5/4=5/4=1¼.
practiceQuestions: Add: ⅖ + ⅓
Subtract: ¾ − ⅖
A boy ate ⅜ of a cake and his sister ate ¼. How much cake did they eat altogether?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Multiplication and Division of Fractions
concepts: Step 1 — Recall: multiplying fractions means multiplying straight across (numerator×numerator, denominator×denominator)
Step 2 — Recall: dividing by a fraction means "flip and multiply" (the reciprocal)
To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and denominators because you are taking a part of another part.
workedExamples: ½ ÷ ¼ = ½ × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2 (makes sense: how many quarters fit into a half? Two.)
practiceQuestions: Multiply: ⅗ × ⅔
Divide: ¾ ÷ ½

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Decimals
concepts: Step 1 — Establish that decimal place value continues the SAME pattern as whole numbers, but going the OTHER direction (tenths, hundredths) after the decimal point
Tens → Units → . → Tenths → Hundredths 3 → 5 → . → 2 → 7 35.27 means 3 tens, 5 units, 2 tenths (2/10), and 7 hundredths (7/100).
Step 1 — Establish the KEY rule: line up the decimal points, so tenths add to tenths, hundredths to hundredths — just like lining up place value columns for whole numbers
workedExamples: 4.35 + 2.7 Line up: 4.35 + 2.70 (write 2.7 as 2.70 to match the columns — this doesn't change its value, just makes lining up clearer) = 7.05
practiceQuestions: What is the value of the digit 4 in 26.489?
Convert ⅖ to a decimal.
Subtract: 9.5 − 3.27

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Percentages (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish "percent" means "out of 100," connecting directly to the decimal/fraction work just done
Percent means “out of 100.” A percentage can be converted to a fraction over 100 or to a decimal by dividing by 100.
To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply the quantity by the percentage written as a fraction or decimal.
practiceQuestions: Convert 40% to a fraction in lowest terms, and to a decimal.
Convert ⅗ to a percentage.
Find 15% of 240.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Money (Nigerian Currency)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish practical transaction skills: total cost, change given, simple budgeting
Money problems require identifying the starting amount, money added or received, and money spent or removed.
In Nigerian currency, 100 kobo = ₦1. Align naira and kobo or use decimal notation consistently.
workedExamples: Ada buys a pencil for ₦150 and an eraser for ₦80. She pays with a ₦500 note. Find her change. Total cost=150+80=₦230. Change=500−230=₦270.
practiceQuestions: A book costs ₦450. If you pay with ₦1,000, find your change.
Musa has ₦2,000 pocket money for the week. He spends ₦300 on Monday, ₦250 on Tuesday. How much does he have left?
A child has ₦7,500 and spends ₦2,875. How much remains?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Measurement — Length, Mass, Capacity
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the base units and conversion method (recall pattern: divide going small→large, multiply going large→small)
Length: 100cm=1m, 1000m=1km. Mass: 1000g=1kg. Capacity: 1000ml=1litre.
Measurement uses agreed units. Before converting, identify the quantity: length, mass, capacity, time, area or volume.
workedExamples: Convert 3.5km to metres: 3.5×1000=3,500m. Convert 2,400g to kg: 2,400÷1000=2.4kg.
3.5 m = 350 cm because 1 m = 100 cm.
practiceQuestions: Convert 6.2m to cm.
Convert 1,800ml to litres.
A bag of rice weighs 2,500g. Express this in kg.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Time
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the 24-hour clock, converting from the familiar 12-hour format
Time can be expressed with clocks, minutes, hours, days and calendar units. Conversion factors must be used carefully: 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Elapsed time is the duration between a start and finish; it can be found by counting forward in manageable steps.
workedExamples: 3:00pm in 24-hour time: add 12 to the hour (since it's "pm" and past 12): 3+12=15:00.
A journey starts at 9:30am and ends at 1:15pm. Find the duration. From 9:30am to 12:00pm = 2hrs 30min. From 12:00pm to 1:15pm = 1hr 15min. Total = 2hr30min+1hr15min = 3hr45min.
practiceQuestions: Convert 7:45pm to 24-hour time.
A class starts at 10:20am and lasts 50 minutes. What time does it end?
Find the elapsed time from 1:45 p.m. to 4:20 p.m.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Perimeter and Area
concepts: Step 1 — Recall: perimeter is total distance around; area is surface covered, counted in unit squares
Perimeter measures the boundary around a flat shape, area measures the surface covered, and volume measures space occupied by a solid. They are different quantities and use different units.
For rectangles, perimeter = 2(length+width) and area = length×width. For rectangular prisms, volume = length×width×height.
workedExamples: Rectangle 8cm by 5cm: Perimeter=2(8+5)=26cm. Area=8×5=40cm².
Rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm: perimeter=2(8+5)=26 cm; area=8×5=40 cm².
practiceQuestions: Find the perimeter and area of a square with side 6cm.
A rectangular garden is 12m by 7m. Find its perimeter and area.
Find the area and perimeter of a 12 cm by 7 cm rectangle.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Basic Shapes and Angles
concepts: Step 1 — Establish angle types by their SIZE range, using a visual clock-hand comparison
Acute angle: less than 90° (a "sharp," small opening). Right angle: exactly 90° (like a square corner). Obtuse angle: more than 90° but less than 180°. Straight angle: exactly 180° (a straight line).
An angle measures turn and is measured in degrees. Acute angles are less than 90°, right angles equal 90°, obtuse angles lie between 90° and 180°.
workedExamples: If one angle on a straight line is 65°, the other is 180°−65°=115°.
A triangle with angles 50° and 60° has third angle 70°.
practiceQuestions: Classify these angles: 45°, 90°, 120°, 180°.
Name a 2D shape with exactly 3 sides, and one with exactly 4 equal sides.
Classify an angle of 135°.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Simple Data Handling
concepts: Step 1 — Establish reading a bar graph: the height of each bar shows the quantity for that category
Data are values collected to answer a question. Read headings, labels and units before using a table or chart.
The mean is total ÷ number of values. The mode is the most frequent value. The median is the middle value after ordering the data.
workedExamples: A bar graph shows: Mango=5 votes, Orange=8 votes, Banana=3 votes. Which fruit was most popular? Orange, since its bar is tallest (8 votes, the highest number).
practiceQuestions: From the data: Football=12, Basketball=7, Swimming=5 — which sport is least popular, and how do you know?
If a tally chart shows |||| | for a count, what number does this represent? (4 full lines + 1 = 5, since tally marks group in 5s)
Find the mean of 5,7,8,10.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Word Problems (Multi-Step Revision)
concepts: A word problem must be translated before it is calculated: identify what is known, what is asked, and the relationship between the quantities.
Underline clue relationships but do not rely on one keyword alone; decide whether the situation describes combining, comparing, equal groups, rates, fractions or another structure.
For multi-step problems, write each intermediate result with its meaning, then check the final answer against the story.
workedExamples: A trader had 3,500 oranges. She sold 1,250 in the morning and 980 in the afternoon. How many oranges are left? Total sold=1,250+980=2,230. Left=3,500−2,230=1,270.
A shop has 240 bottles, sells 85 in the morning and 67 later. Total sold=152; remaining=240−152=88.
practiceQuestions: A tank holds 500 litres. If 180 litres are used in the morning and 95 litres in the evening, how much water remains?
Musa has ₦3,000. He buys 3 books at ₦450 each. How much money does he have left?
A farmer packs 1,260 oranges equally into 9 baskets. How many per basket?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Whole Numbers — Place Value to Millions/Billions, Standard Form (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Extend Primary 5's place value work to millions, using the same grouping-in-3s method already established
Step 2 — Introduce standard form as a preview (fully developed later in JSS, but the CONCEPT starts here)
Standard form writes a number as (a number 1-10) × a power of 10. 4,000,000 = 4×10⁶ (since we move the decimal 6 places).
workedExamples: Read 4,250,000: group as 4 | 250 | 000 → four million, two hundred and fifty thousand.
In 4,582,731 the digit 8 is in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 80,000.
practiceQuestions: Read 7,300,000 in words.
Write 3,000,000 in standard form.
What is the value of 7 in 2,734,105?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Approximation and Estimation
concepts: Step 1 — Recall the rounding rule (5 rounds up) and apply it at larger scales
Approximation replaces a number with a nearby simpler value according to a stated place value or number of significant figures.
To round, look at the digit immediately to the right of the place being kept: 5 or more rounds up; below 5 stays.
workedExamples: Round 456,789 to the nearest ten-thousand. Look at the thousands digit (6): since 6≥5, round the ten-thousands digit up: 460,000.
48,763 rounded to the nearest thousand is 49,000.
practiceQuestions: Round 82,349 to the nearest thousand.
Estimate the total cost of 3 items priced ₦1,980, ₦2,950, and ₦4,120 by first rounding each to the nearest thousand.
Round 6,748 to the nearest hundred.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Factors, Multiples, LCM and HCF (Full Method)
concepts: Step 1 — Recall factors/multiples from Primary 5, now applying the full LCM/HCF method (listing AND prime factorization)
A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is produced by multiplying the number by a whole number.
HCF is the greatest factor shared by the numbers; LCM is the smallest positive multiple shared by them.
workedExamples: Find the LCM of 8 and 12. Multiples of 8: 8,16,24... Multiples of 12: 12,24... First common: 24.
Find the HCF of 18 and 24. Factors of 18: 1,2,3,6,9,18. Factors of 24: 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24. Common: 1,2,3,6. Highest: 6.
practiceQuestions: Find the LCM of 6 and 9.
Find the HCF of 20 and 30.
Two bells ring every 6 and 8 minutes. When will they next ring together? (an LCM word problem)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Fractions — Full Operations and Word Problems
concepts: Step 1 — Consolidate all four operations, then apply to multi-step word problems
A fraction represents equal parts of a whole or of a quantity. The denominator tells how many equal parts make the whole; the numerator tells how many parts are considered.
Equivalent fractions name the same quantity with different-sized equal parts. Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number to create an equivalent fraction.
workedExamples: A tank is ⅔ full. If ¼ of the remaining space is filled, what fraction of the tank is now full? Remaining space initially = 1−⅔=⅓. ¼ of that remaining space is filled: ¼×⅓=1/12. New total filled = ⅔+1/12. Common denominator=12: ⅔=8/12. 8/12+1/12=9/12=¾.
3/4 means 3 of 4 equal parts. 6/8 is equivalent because both numerator and denominator were doubled.
practiceQuestions: Add: 2⅓ + 1¾

A trader sold ⅗ of his oranges in the morning and ⅙ of the remainder in the afternoon. What fraction of the total did he sell in the afternoon? (careful: ⅙ of the REMAINDER, not of the original total)
Write an equivalent fraction for 5/6.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Ratio and Proportion (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish ratio as comparing quantities directly, connecting to the sharing method
A ratio compares quantities using equal-sized parts. Simplify a ratio by dividing every term by the same common factor.
In direct proportion, quantities change by the same scale factor; if one doubles, the corresponding quantity doubles.
workedExamples: Share 60 sweets between two children in the ratio 2:3. Total parts=5. Each part=60÷5=12. First share=2×12=24. Second share=3×12=36.
Share ₦1,000 in ratio 2:3. Total parts=5; one part=₦200; shares are ₦400 and ₦600.
practiceQuestions: Share ₦800 between two people in the ratio 3:5.
Simplify the ratio 12:16 to its lowest terms.
Simplify 18:24.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Decimals — Full Operations and Word Problems
concepts: Decimals extend place value to tenths, hundredths and thousandths. A digit’s value depends on its position relative to the decimal point.
When adding or subtracting decimals, align decimal points so equal place values are combined.
Fractions, decimals and percentages can describe the same quantity, so converting between forms helps check answers.
workedExamples: 3.2 × 1.5. Ignore decimals first: 32×15=480. Now count total decimal places in the original numbers (1 in 3.2, 1 in 1.5 = 2 total): place the decimal point 2 places from the right in 480: 4.80.
practiceQuestions: Multiply: 2.4 × 3.6
Divide: 6.4 ÷ 0.8 (hint: multiply both numbers by 10 to remove the decimal, then divide normally: 64÷8)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Percentages — Full Treatment
concepts: Step 1 — Recall percentage-of-a-quantity and percentage change, now with profit/loss framing
Percent means “out of 100.” A percentage can be converted to a fraction over 100 or to a decimal by dividing by 100.
To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply the quantity by the percentage written as a fraction or decimal.
workedExamples: A trader buys an item for ₦800 and sells it for ₦1,000. Find the percentage profit. Profit=1,000−800=₦200. Percentage profit=(200/800)×100=25%.
practiceQuestions: A shopkeeper buys a shirt for ₦1,500 and sells it for ₦1,800. Find the percentage profit.
A price is reduced by 20% from ₦5,000. Find the new price.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Simple Interest (Introductory)
concepts: Simple interest is the extra money paid or earned on an original principal for a stated time at a stated rate.
For simple interest, SI = P×R×T/100, where P is principal, R is annual rate percent, and T is time in years.
The amount after simple interest is principal plus interest. Keep the rate and time units consistent.
workedExamples: Find the simple interest on ₦10,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum. I=(P×R×T)/100=(10,000×5×2)/100=₦1,000.
practiceQuestions: Find the simple interest on ₦20,000 for 3 years at 4% per annum.
Find the simple interest on ₦15,000 at 4% for 3 years.
Find the amount on ₦6,000 at 5% for 2 years.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Algebra (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish a letter standing for an unknown number, and solving simple one-step equations
A letter in algebra can represent an unknown number. An equation states that two expressions have the same value.
To solve an equation, keep the balance: whatever operation is done to one side must be done to the other side.
workedExamples: Solve: x + 7 = 15. Subtract 7 from both sides: x=8.
practiceQuestions: Solve: x − 5 = 12
Solve: 3x = 21
A number added to 9 gives 20. Find the number (translate to an equation first).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Directed Numbers (Introductory)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish negative numbers using a real-world reference: temperature below zero, or debt
Directed numbers include positive numbers, zero and negative numbers. A number line shows their order clearly.
Moving right on a number line increases value; moving left decreases value. A negative number closer to zero is greater than one farther left.
workedExamples: The temperature was −3°C and rose by 8°C. Find the new temperature: −3+8=5°C.
−3 is greater than −7 because −3 lies to the right of −7 on the number line.
practiceQuestions: Calculate: −5 + 9
Calculate: 4 − 10
Order −5,2,0,−1 from least to greatest.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Measurement — Full Conversions and Word Problems
concepts: Measurement uses agreed units. Before converting, identify the quantity: length, mass, capacity, time, area or volume.
A conversion changes the unit name without changing the actual quantity. Multiply when moving to smaller units and divide when moving to larger units, using the correct conversion factor.
Keep compound and square units distinct: 1 m = 100 cm, but 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
workedExamples: A tailor has 5.5m of cloth. Each shirt needs 1.25m. How many complete shirts can be made? 5.5÷1.25=4.4 → 4 complete shirts (0.4 of a shirt's worth of cloth remains, not enough for a 5th).
3.5 m = 350 cm because 1 m = 100 cm.
practiceQuestions: A rope is 12.6m long. If it's cut into pieces of 0.9m each, how many pieces can be made?
Convert 4.75 m to cm.
Convert 3,250 mL to litres.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Perimeter, Area, and Volume
concepts: Perimeter measures the boundary around a flat shape, area measures the surface covered, and volume measures space occupied by a solid. They are different quantities and use different units.
For rectangles, perimeter = 2(length+width) and area = length×width. For rectangular prisms, volume = length×width×height.
Always write the correct unit: length units for perimeter, square units for area, cubic units for volume.
workedExamples: A box is 8cm×5cm×4cm. Find its volume: 8×5×4=160cm³.
Rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm: perimeter=2(8+5)=26 cm; area=8×5=40 cm².
practiceQuestions: Find the area of a triangle with base 14cm and height 8cm.
Find the volume of a cuboid 10cm×6cm×5cm.
Find the area and perimeter of a 12 cm by 7 cm rectangle.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Angles and Basic Geometry
concepts: An angle measures turn and is measured in degrees. Acute angles are less than 90°, right angles equal 90°, obtuse angles lie between 90° and 180°.
Shapes are classified by properties such as number of sides, equal sides, parallel sides and angle sizes, not merely by how a drawing looks.
The angles on a straight line add to 180°, and the interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
workedExamples: Angles on a straight line: 65° and x°. Find x. x=180−65=115°.
If one angle on a straight line is 65°, the other is 180°−65°=115°.
practiceQuestions: Find the missing angle: two angles on a straight line are 40° and x°.
Name a shape with 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
Classify an angle of 135°.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Data Handling and Statistics
concepts: Step 1 — Introduce average (mean) as "sharing the total equally"
Data are values collected to answer a question. Read headings, labels and units before using a table or chart.
The mean is total ÷ number of values. The mode is the most frequent value. The median is the middle value after ordering the data.
workedExamples: Find the average of 4, 7, 9, 12. Total=4+7+9+12=32. Average=32÷4=8.
practiceQuestions: Find the average of 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
A pie chart shows 90° for a category out of a total of 40 people surveyed. How many people does this represent? (90/360=¼; ¼×40=10)
Find the mean of 5,7,8,10.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Speed, Distance, and Time (Introductory)
concepts: Speed compares distance travelled with time taken: speed = distance ÷ time.
The three related formulas are distance = speed×time, speed = distance÷time, and time = distance÷speed.
Convert time units before substituting into a formula; for example 30 minutes = 0.5 hour if speed is in km/h.
workedExamples: A car travels 120km in 2 hours. Find its speed: 120÷2=60km/h.
At 60 km/h for 2.5 h, distance=60×2.5=150 km.
practiceQuestions: A cyclist travels 45km in 3 hours. Find the speed.
A car travels at 60km/h for 2.5 hours. Find the distance covered (Distance=Speed×Time=60×2.5).
Find the distance travelled at 80 km/h for 45 minutes.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Full Revision — NCEE-Style Mixed Word Problems
concepts: A word problem must be translated before it is calculated: identify what is known, what is asked, and the relationship between the quantities.
Underline clue relationships but do not rely on one keyword alone; decide whether the situation describes combining, comparing, equal groups, rates, fractions or another structure.
For multi-step problems, write each intermediate result with its meaning, then check the final answer against the story.
workedExamples: Musa had ₦5,000. He spent ⅖ on books and 15% of the remainder on transport. How much does he have left? Spent on books=⅖×5,000=₦2,000. Remainder=5,000−2,000=₦3,000. Spent on transport=15%×3,000=₦450. Left=3,000−450=₦2,550.
A shop has 240 bottles, sells 85 in the morning and 67 later. Total sold=152; remaining=240−152=88.
practiceQuestions: A trader had 240 oranges. She sold ¾ of them and gave away 20% of the remainder to a neighbor. How many oranges does she have left?
A rectangular field is 60m by 40m. Find its area, then find how much it would cost to fence it at ₦500 per metre.
A farmer packs 1,260 oranges equally into 9 baskets. How many per basket?

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Number Patterns and Sequences
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the core method for ANY sequence puzzle: find the RULE connecting consecutive terms by testing simple operations first (add, subtract, multiply)
A number pattern is controlled by a rule. Test differences, ratios or alternating operations rather than guessing from the last two numbers only.
For changing-difference patterns, calculate consecutive differences and inspect how those differences change.
workedExamples: 1 (simple addition pattern): 2, 5, 8, 11, ___? Test: 5−2=3, 8−5=3, 11−8=3 — consistent rule: add 3 each time. Next: 11+3=14.

2 (multiplication pattern): 3, 6, 12, 24, ___? Test differences first: 6−3=3, 12−6=6, 24−12=12 — NOT constant, so addition isn't the rule. Test ratios instead: 6÷3=2, 12÷6=2, 24÷12=2 — consistent: multiply by 2 each time. Next: 24×2=48.

3 (a trickier alternating pattern, testing beyond the first guess) 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, ___? This doesn't fit a single simple add/multiply rule across ALL terms. Look for TWO interleaved patterns: positions 1,3,5 (1,2,3 — adding 1 each time) and positions 2,4,6 (4,5,6 — adding 1 each time). The 7th term continues the first pattern: 3+1=4.
practiceQuestions: Find the next number: 4, 8, 12, 16, ___?
Find the next number: 1, 3, 9, 27, ___? (test differences first, then ratios if differences don't work)
Find the next number: 20, 17, 14, 11, ___?
Find the missing number: 2, 4, 8, ___, 32 (test the rule using the numbers you DO have on both sides of the gap)

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Relationships Between Numbers
concepts: Step 1 — Establish odd/even, factors, and multiples as tools for spotting relationships in puzzles
A coded-number puzzle hides a rule connecting inputs to outputs.
Test each candidate rule against every given example; a rule that fits only one example may be coincidence.
workedExamples: "Which number does not belong: 12, 18, 24, 25?" Test: 12,18,24 are all multiples of 6 (12=6×2, 18=6×3, 24=6×4), but 25 is not (25÷6 doesn't divide evenly). 25 is the odd one out.
If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, rule 2a+b fits both: 6+4=10 and 10+2=12.
practiceQuestions: Which number does not belong: 15, 20, 25, 27? (test what the others have in common first)
Which number does not belong: 8, 16, 24, 30? (hint: test multiples of a specific number)
Test a rule against two examples before using it.

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Simple Logical Number Puzzles
concepts: Step 1 — Establish reading a puzzle's given rule CAREFULLY and applying it exactly, testing with the given example before solving the actual question
A coded-number puzzle hides a rule connecting inputs to outputs.
Test each candidate rule against every given example; a rule that fits only one example may be coincidence.
workedExamples: "If ☆ means 'add 3 then double,' find 4☆." Apply step by step: 4+3=7, then double: 7×2=14. So 4☆=14.
If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, rule 2a+b fits both: 6+4=10 and 10+2=12.
practiceQuestions: If ◇ means "multiply by 2 then subtract 1," find 5◇.
If a rule says "double the number and add 5," and the result is 15, what was the original number? (work backwards: 15−5=10, then 10÷2=5)
Test a rule against two examples before using it.

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Word-Based Number Problems (Pattern Recognition)
concepts: A number pattern is controlled by a rule. Test differences, ratios or alternating operations rather than guessing from the last two numbers only.
For changing-difference patterns, calculate consecutive differences and inspect how those differences change.
Confirm a proposed rule on more than one step before using it to predict the next term.
workedExamples: "A pattern of chairs is arranged: 1 chair in row 1, 3 chairs in row 2, 5 chairs in row 3. How many chairs in row 5?" Pattern: odd numbers increasing by 2 each row (1,3,5,7,9...). Row 5 = 9 chairs.
1,2,4,7,11 has differences 1,2,3,4, so next difference is 5 and next term is 16.
practiceQuestions: A pattern of tiles: 2, 4, 6, 8... How many tiles in the 6th position?
A saving pattern: Week 1 save ₦100, Week 2 save ₦150, Week 3 save ₦200. If the pattern continues, how much is saved in Week 5?
Find the next term: 3,6,11,18,27,...

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Number Sequences (Full Range — Arithmetic, Geometric, Mixed-Rule)
concepts: A number pattern is controlled by a rule. Test differences, ratios or alternating operations rather than guessing from the last two numbers only.
For changing-difference patterns, calculate consecutive differences and inspect how those differences change.
Confirm a proposed rule on more than one step before using it to predict the next term.
workedExamples: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, ___? Test differences: 2−1=1, 4−2=2, 7−4=3, 11−7=4 — the DIFFERENCES themselves increase by 1 each time. Next difference=5: 11+5=16.
1,2,4,7,11 has differences 1,2,3,4, so next difference is 5 and next term is 16.
practiceQuestions: Find the next number: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ___? (test the differences of the differences, as shown above)
Find the next number: 100, 50, 25, 12.5, ___?
Find the next term: 3,6,11,18,27,...

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Relationships Disguised as Puzzles
concepts: A coded-number puzzle hides a rule connecting inputs to outputs.
Test each candidate rule against every given example; a rule that fits only one example may be coincidence.
Once confirmed, apply exactly the same order of operations to the new input.
workedExamples: "If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, find the rule and use it to find 6☆3." Test candidate rules against BOTH examples before committing to one: Try "a+b": 3+4=7 (not 10) — rejected immediately, since it fails the first example. Try "2a+b": 2(3)+4=10 ✓ matches the first example. Check against the second: 2(5)+2=12 ✓ matches too! Since this rule fits BOTH given examples consistently, it's confirmed. Apply to find 6☆3: 2(6)+3=15. This is the real exam skill: test a candidate rule against ALL given examples before trusting it — a rule that only fits ONE example could easily be a coincidence, not the actual pattern.
If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, rule 2a+b fits both: 6+4=10 and 10+2=12.
practiceQuestions: If 2★3=8 and 4★1=6, test at least two candidate rules against BOTH examples before finding the one that fits consistently, then find 5★2.
If a rule states "double the first number and subtract the second," and 6◆2 uses this rule, find the result.
Test a rule against two examples before using it.

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Fractions/Decimals/Percentages in Reasoning Puzzles
concepts: A coded-number puzzle hides a rule connecting inputs to outputs.
Test each candidate rule against every given example; a rule that fits only one example may be coincidence.
Once confirmed, apply exactly the same order of operations to the new input.
workedExamples: "If ⅓ of a number is 15, find the number." Reasoning: if ⅓ = 15, the whole number = 15×3 = 45.
If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, rule 2a+b fits both: 6+4=10 and 10+2=12.
practiceQuestions: If ¼ of a number is 12, find the number.
If 20% of a number is 8, find the number.
Test a rule against two examples before using it.

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Algebraic Reasoning Puzzles
concepts: A coded-number puzzle hides a rule connecting inputs to outputs.
Test each candidate rule against every given example; a rule that fits only one example may be coincidence.
Once confirmed, apply exactly the same order of operations to the new input.
workedExamples: "I think of a number, double it, and add 5. The result is 17. Find the number." (2x+5=17 → 2x=12 → x=6)
If 3☆4=10 and 5☆2=12, rule 2a+b fits both: 6+4=10 and 10+2=12.
practiceQuestions: A number is tripled and 4 is subtracted, giving 20. Find the number.
Test a rule against two examples before using it.
Create a rule that fits two given input-output pairs.

topics.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
topics.title: Time, Speed, Measurement Reasoning
concepts: Identify the quantities and units before calculating.
Convert units first when the formula uses a different unit, such as minutes to hours for km/h.
Use the relationship distance=speed×time and rearrange it only after identifying what is unknown.
workedExamples: "A car travels at 40km/h. How far does it travel in 45 minutes?" Convert 45 min to hours: 45/60=¾hr. Distance=speed×time=40×¾=30km.
practiceQuestions: A train travels at 80km/h for 30 minutes. Find the distance covered.
Find distance at 60 km/h for 20 minutes.
Convert 90 minutes to hours.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Odd-One-Out (Word Groups)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the method: find what MOST of the words have in common first, then identify which one breaks that pattern
Odd-one-out questions depend on a grouping rule shared by most items.
Test more than one possible rule and choose the one that creates the clearest consistent group.
workedExamples: "Rose, Tulip, Sunflower, Carrot" → Test: Rose, Tulip, Sunflower are all flowers. Carrot is a vegetable/root. Odd one out: Carrot.

"Whale, Shark, Dolphin, Salmon" → All live in water, so that's not the distinguishing feature. Test another category: Whale and Dolphin are mammals; Shark and Salmon are fish. This puzzle actually needs the SPECIFIC instruction "which does not belong with the others" to be based on ONE clear odd-one-out — if the intended answer is based on "mammal vs fish," then EITHER Whale/Dolphin (mammals) are the pair that stands apart from Shark/Salmon (fish), OR vice versa, depending on which group is "the odd ones." This shows why reading the exact instruction matters — sometimes there are two valid groupings, and identifying the SPECIFIC contrast intended requires elimination based on the answer options given.
practiceQuestions: Find the odd one out: "Circle, Square, Triangle, Ball" and explain your reasoning.
Find the odd one out: "Doctor, Teacher, Nurse, Hospital" (hint: three are people/professions, one is a place).
Find the odd one out: swim, run, jump, strong.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Word Analogies
concepts: Step 1 — Establish the METHOD: identify the RELATIONSHIP between the first pair, then apply the SAME relationship to find the missing word
Understand every word first.
Identify the relationship or rule.
workedExamples: "Finger is to Hand as Toe is to ___?" Relationship: a finger is PART OF a hand. Applying the same relationship: a toe is part of a ___? Answer: Foot.
"Pen is to Write as Knife is to ___?" Relationship: a pen is USED TO write. A knife is used to ___? Answer: Cut.
"Rose is to Flower as Mango is to ___?" Relationship: a rose is a TYPE OF flower. A mango is a type of ___? Answer: Fruit.
practiceQuestions: Complete: "Hand is to Glove as Foot is to ___?"
Complete: "Bird is to Nest as Bee is to ___?"
Complete: "Cold is to Ice as Hot is to ___?" (identify the relationship type first: is this cause/effect, part/whole, or opposite?)

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Word Classification and Grouping
concepts: Step 1 — Establish sorting words into categories by shared properties
Classification groups words by a shared meaning, function, grammar or other clear property.
The rule must fit every member of the group; advanced questions may contain two hidden group rules.
workedExamples: Sort into two groups: "Lion, Rose, Tiger, Sunflower, Elephant, Tulip" → Group 1 (animals): Lion, Tiger, Elephant. Group 2 (flowers): Rose, Sunflower, Tulip.
Rose, lily, tulip are flowers; carrot, cabbage, spinach are vegetables.
practiceQuestions: Sort into two groups: "Apple, Chair, Banana, Table, Orange, Bed" (what are the two categories?).
Which word does NOT belong in this group, and why: "Red, Blue, Green, Triangle, Yellow"?
Sort six words into two named groups.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Basic Coding (Letter/Number Substitution)
concepts: Step 1 — Establish that a "code" follows a FIXED, consistent rule that must be discovered by testing
Coding replaces letters or words according to a rule. Decode by identifying and reversing the same rule.
Keep repeated letters consistent and track shifts carefully through the alphabet.
workedExamples: "If CAT is coded as DBU, what is DOG coded as?" Test the rule: C→D (shift forward by 1 letter), A→B (shift by 1), T→U (shift by 1). Consistent rule: shift each letter forward by 1. Apply to DOG: D→E, O→P, G→H. Coded as: EPH.
Shift each letter forward by 3: CAT → FDW.
practiceQuestions: If DOG is coded as EPH (using the same "shift forward by 1" rule), what would CAT be coded as? (Check your answer against the worked example above.)
If 1=A, 2=B, 3=C... what number represents the letter E?
Code DOG by shifting each letter forward 2.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Word Analogies (Full Range)
concepts: Step 1 — Categorize the DIFFERENT types of relationships analogies can use, testing each type explicitly

- Synonym-based: "Happy is to Joyful as Sad is to ___?" → Unhappy/Sorrowful - Antonym-based: "Hot is to Cold as Day is to ___?" → Night - Part-to-whole: "Page is to Book as Brick is to ___?" → Wall/House - Function-based: "Scissors is to Cut as Broom is to ___?" → Sweep - Category-based: "Rose is to Flower as Lion is to ___?" → Animal
Understand every word first.
workedExamples: "Doctor is to Hospital as Teacher is to ___?" Relationship: a doctor WORKS IN a hospital. Apply: a teacher works in a ___? Answer: School.
Work one example and name the relationship.
practiceQuestions: Identify the relationship type, then complete: "Fish is to Water as Bird is to ___?"
Complete: "Author is to Book as Sculptor is to ___?"
Complete: "Kind is to Cruel as Brave is to ___?" (identify: synonym or antonym-based?)

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Odd-One-Out (Advanced)
concepts: Odd-one-out questions depend on a grouping rule shared by most items.
Test more than one possible rule and choose the one that creates the clearest consistent group.
State why the odd item fails the group rule; do not stop at naming it.
workedExamples: "Triangle, Square, Circle, Pentagon" — test: number of sides. Triangle=3, Square=4, Pentagon=5 all have straight sides and a countable number of sides; Circle has NO straight sides/no countable sides. Odd one out: Circle.
Triangle, square and pentagon have straight sides; circle does not, so circle is odd.
practiceQuestions: Find the odd one out: "Novel, Poem, Play, Author" (three are TYPES of writing, one is a person).
Find the odd one out: "Swim, Run, Jump, Strong" (three are actions/verbs, one is a description/adjective).
Find the odd one out: swim, run, jump, strong.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Coding and Decoding (Full)
concepts: Coding replaces letters or words according to a rule. Decode by identifying and reversing the same rule.
Keep repeated letters consistent and track shifts carefully through the alphabet.
Test the rule on a known part before applying it to the whole word.
workedExamples: "If APPLE is coded as 12345 where A=1, P=2, P=2, L=3... wait — establish the actual rule: each DIFFERENT letter gets the NEXT available number in order of first appearance: A=1, P=2 (first P), P=2 (repeat, same number), L=3, E=4. So APPLE=12234."
Shift each letter forward by 3: CAT → FDW.
practiceQuestions: Using the same "number letters in order of first appearance" rule, code the word "BANANA."
If a code shifts each letter BACK by 2 (so encoding D→B, O→M, G→E, meaning DOG becomes BME), decode "BME" by reversing the shift (moving each letter FORWARD by 2) to find the original word.
Code DOG by shifting each letter forward 2.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Sentence and Word Sequencing
concepts: Sequencing arranges words or events according to a logical relationship such as time, cause and effect, size or process.
Look for an event that must happen first and another that can only happen after something else.
After arranging, read the full sequence to check for impossible jumps or reversed cause and effect.
workedExamples: Arrange in logical order: "He ate breakfast. / He woke up. / He brushed his teeth. / He went to school." Correct order: He woke up → He brushed his teeth → He ate breakfast → He went to school (following the natural sequence of a morning routine).
Clouds gather → rain starts → rain stops → sun appears is a sensible time sequence.
practiceQuestions: Arrange in logical order: "The rain stopped. / Dark clouds gathered. / The sun came out. / It started raining."
Arrange four morning activities logically.
Explain which event must come first in a short process.

topics.subject: Verbal Reasoning
topics.title: Word Classification and Grouping (Advanced)
concepts: Word classification means placing words into groups because they share a clear property. The important skill is not merely making groups; it is stating the rule that makes every member belong.
Start by looking for possible dimensions such as meaning, function, size, sound, part of speech, place, category or degree. Do not assume the first similarity you notice is the intended one.
A valid grouping rule must fit every word placed in that group. If one word does not fit, either the rule is wrong or the word belongs elsewhere.
Advanced classification may contain two different hidden dimensions. Name both groups explicitly before sorting the words.
Some words can fit more than one broad category, so prefer the grouping that explains all the words cleanly and creates balanced, meaningful sets.
After grouping, perform a reverse check: choose one word from each group and explain why swapping them would break the rule.
workedExamples: Sort: Whisper, Shout, Elephant, Mouse, Murmur, Giant. First search for dimensions. Whisper, shout and murmur describe ways or volumes of speaking/sound. Elephant, mouse and giant relate to beings described strongly by size. The two rules explain all six words.
Sort: Rose, Lily, Carrot, Cabbage, Tulip, Spinach. Rose, lily and tulip are flowers; carrot, cabbage and spinach are vegetables. The category rule is consistent for every word.
Sort: Run, Swim, Happy, Angry, Jump, Sad. Run, swim and jump are actions; happy, angry and sad describe feelings or states. The grammatical/meaning distinction separates the sets.
practiceQuestions: Sort into two groups and name each rule: Whisper, Shout, Elephant, Mouse, Murmur, Giant.
Group these words and explain your rule: Mango, Orange, Lion, Goat, Banana, Cow.
Which word would break this group and why: run, jump, swim, beautiful?
Create six words that can be sorted into two groups of three, then state both group rules.
